transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start off, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?

Yeah… so, the main thing that made me finally come in is that I keep running into this wall with work that needs sustained, sit-down thinking. I’m a health services manager, so there are these tasks that really do matter—monthly reports, planning details for a multi-site health event, things where I have to sit there and organize information and think through steps—and I just… I don’t know, it feels like my brain refuses to engage.

It’s not that I don’t understand the work, and it’s not that I don’t care. I do care, which is part of why it’s frustrating. But when I know something is going to take real mental effort for a while, I find myself putting it off, circling around it, doing smaller things first, telling myself I’ll start after one more email or after I get coffee or after a meeting. And then suddenly I’ve lost a lot of time, and the important thing is still sitting there.

That’s probably the biggest reason I’m here—because I know these things matter, but I keep avoiding them like I’m hitting a wall.

Have you experienced this kind of difficulty starting and sustaining focus on effortful tasks for as long as you can remember, even back in school, or is this something that started more recently in adulthood?

No, it definitely goes way back. I mean, when you ask that, my mind goes right to elementary school. I was always told I was bright—like teachers would say to my parents, “He’s smart, he understands it”—but then there was always the “but.” But he’s staring out the window, but he’s daydreaming, but he can’t seem to keep track of his papers.

I remember worksheets just disappearing. Not even in some dramatic way—I’d have them, and then they’d be crumpled in the bottom of my backpack, or left in my desk, or I’d forget they existed. And homework was a whole thing. I could do it if my mother basically checked my backpack every night and made sure I had what I needed and then made sure it got put back in the folder. If she didn’t, there was a decent chance I’d either forget to do it or do it and not turn it in, which is almost more embarrassing because it makes no sense.

So, yeah, it doesn’t feel like something that suddenly started in adulthood. Work has made it more obvious and more costly, I guess, but the pattern was there when I was a kid.

Growing up and even now, have you often felt restless, fidgety, or like you had to keep moving, or found yourself acting impulsively—like interrupting others or blurting things out—rather than just having trouble focusing?

I wouldn’t say I’m someone who’s constantly needing to move, exactly. The thing I do notice—more than the physical restlessness—is that I can talk too much in certain situations.

Like, if I realize I’ve dropped the ball on something, especially at work, I get nervous and I start over-explaining. Say I made a scheduling mistake, or I missed some detail and now someone’s asking about it—I’ll start explaining what happened, and then I keep adding context, and then more context, and I can almost see on the other person’s face that they already understand the point. But I’m still talking. It’s like I’m trying to prove that I wasn’t being careless, or that there was a reason, or that I know it mattered.

And sometimes afterward I think, “Why did I keep going? They got it after the first two sentences.” But in the moment I feel anxious and I just sort of fill the space with too much explanation. So yeah, not so much blurting things out randomly, but excessive talking when I’m nervous about having messed something up—that definitely happens.

Outside of these work situations where you've made a mistake, do you also find yourself worrying excessively or feeling anxious about a lot of different things in your daily life—like your health, family, or finances—most days, even when nothing specific has gone wrong?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I worry about things, sure—like anyone does, I think—but I don’t know that I’d describe myself as worrying about everything most days when nothing’s actually happening.

The anxiety I notice most is usually tied to a specific thing, like realizing I missed something or I’m behind, and then I get that kind of pressure in my chest and I start replaying how it happened or what someone’s going to think. But if you’re asking whether I’m just generally worried all the time about health or money or family, like it’s running in the background constantly… I don’t think so. At least that’s not the main thing I’ve noticed.

It’s more like I get anxious when there’s a concrete reason, especially when I feel like I’ve messed up or might disappoint someone. Otherwise I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around worrying most days for no reason.

Do you also notice this kind of forgetfulness or trouble staying organized in other parts of your life outside of work—like losing track of personal items, missing appointments, or forgetting everyday tasks at home?

Yeah, unfortunately, yes. It’s not only a work thing. I wish I could say it was just because my job has a lot of moving parts, but it shows up outside of that too.

Like with volunteer stuff and community events, I’ll mean to return someone’s call, and I’ll even think, “Okay, I need to call them back after lunch,” and then somehow the day just goes by and I don’t do it. Then two days later I’ll see their name again or they’ll follow up, and I get that sinking feeling because I didn’t ignore them on purpose—I just completely lost track of it.

Small errands for events are another one. I’ll agree to pick something up or drop something off, and unless it’s written down in exactly the right place or someone reminds me, it can slip. Not every single time, but enough that it’s embarrassing.

And I’ve had once or twice where a community meeting just completely slipped my mind until someone texted me, like, “Are you still coming?” And then I’m scrambling and apologizing because I genuinely had intended to be there. It makes me feel unreliable, even though I’m not trying to be.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of inattentive symptoms—task avoidance/procrastination on effortful cognitive tasks, losing track of items/papers, forgetfulness in daily responsibilities (calls, errands, appointments), and needing external structure (parental checking) to complete homework. These symptoms persist into adulthood across multiple settings (work, volunteer/community life) and cause functional impairment (missed commitments, work inefficiency, embarrassment). Mild hyperactive-impulsive features are present (excessive talking/over-explaining when anxious about mistakes) but are less prominent than inattentive symptoms, and do not meet full criteria for combined presentation given the primary inattentive burden. Anxiety is present but appears secondary/situational (tied to specific perceived failures) rather than diffuse, excessive worry across domains, making GAD less likely as primary diagnosis; it's better explained as a reaction to ADHD-related functional difficulties.
